title: Midol and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Which Midol You Have Matters
excerpt: Can you drink on Midol? It depends on the formula. How acetaminophen, ibuprofen, naproxen, caffeine, and antihistamine versions interact with alcohol, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you take Midol with alcohol? It depends on which Midol you have. Liver vs stomach risks, the caffeine and PM add-ons, safe timing, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** whether Midol and alcohol are a risky mix depends almost entirely on *which* Midol you have. "Midol" is a brand name, not a single drug. Some Midol products are built around **acetaminophen** (the drug in Tylenol), which puts the strain on your liver. Others are built around **ibuprofen** or **naproxen**, which put the strain on your stomach and kidneys. Many also add **caffeine**, a **sedating antihistamine**, or a **mild water pill**, and each of those interacts with alcohol in its own way. For most healthy adults, one normal dose the morning after a couple of drinks is unlikely to cause harm. The problems come from taking more than the label allows, taking it while you're still drinking, stacking it with other products that contain the same drug, and regular heavy drinking.

**The quick rules:** Turn the box over and read the Drug Facts panel before anything else. If it says acetaminophen, treat it exactly like Tylenol. If it says ibuprofen or naproxen sodium, treat it like Advil or Aleve. Don't take any Midol while you're actively drinking, and don't take it at bedtime "to get ahead of" a hangover or cramps. If you have 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using it at all. If you think you or someone else took too much of an acetaminophen product, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) right away, even if they feel fine.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the warnings printed on over-the-counter labels. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the exact product you have. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining Midol with alcohol if** you drink 3 or more drinks most days, have liver, kidney, or stomach problems, take blood thinners or other prescription medicines, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. **Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or 911** if you may have taken more than the labeled dose, or if you notice vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, severe stomach pain, yellow skin or eyes, or unusual confusion after taking Midol.

## First, Check Which Midol You Have

This is the single most useful thing you can do, and it takes ten seconds. The Midol line has changed over the years and includes several different formulas. The name on the front of the box ("Complete," "Long Lasting," "PM," "Liquid Gels," "Extended Relief," "Bloat") tells you very little. The **active ingredients** listed in the Drug Facts box on the back tell you everything.

Here are the ingredients you're likely to find, and what each one means if you've been drinking:

| Active ingredient you see on the label | What it does | Main concern with alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| **Acetaminophen** (sometimes listed as APAP) | Pain and fever relief | Liver. Same chemistry as Tylenol. |
| **Ibuprofen** | Pain relief, reduces inflammation and cramping | Stomach irritation and bleeding, kidney strain when dehydrated |
| **Naproxen sodium** | Longer-lasting pain relief, reduces inflammation | Same as ibuprofen, and it stays in your body longer |
| **Caffeine** | Mild pain-reliever booster, reduces fatigue | Masks how drunk you feel, worsens sleep, adds to dehydration |
| **Pyrilamine maleate** | Antihistamine, marketed for water-weight bloating | Drowsiness stacks with alcohol |
| **Diphenhydramine** (in "PM" versions) | Sleep aid antihistamine | Strong drowsiness and impairment with alcohol |
| **Pamabrom** | Mild diuretic (water pill) for bloating | Adds to alcohol's dehydrating effect |

The best-known product, **Midol Complete**, has for many years combined acetaminophen, caffeine, and pyrilamine maleate in each caplet. That makes it a three-way interaction with alcohol: a liver question, a stimulant question, and a drowsiness question all at once. But don't assume your box matches. Formulas and names change, store-brand "menstrual relief" products copy different versions, and the box in your bathroom cabinet may be years old. Read the label you actually have.

## Acetaminophen Midol and Alcohol: The Liver Risk

If your Midol contains acetaminophen, everything that applies to Tylenol and alcohol applies here. We cover the chemistry in detail in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol), but here is the plain-words version.

Your liver handles most of each acetaminophen dose safely and sends it out in your urine. A small slice goes down a different route, through a liver enzyme called **CYP2E1**, and that route produces a toxic by-product called **NAPQI**. Normally your liver neutralizes NAPQI right away using an antioxidant called **glutathione**. Liver damage happens when NAPQI is made faster than glutathione can clean it up.

Alcohol pushes on both sides of that balance:

- **Regular heavy drinking increases CYP2E1.** That's the same enzyme that makes NAPQI, so more of each dose gets turned into the toxic by-product.
- **Heavy drinking and skipped meals lower glutathione.** That leaves less capacity to neutralize NAPQI. A night of drinking followed by a morning with no breakfast is a poor time to load up on acetaminophen.

The US Food and Drug Administration requires a liver warning on over-the-counter acetaminophen products. It says severe liver damage may occur if you take more than the maximum daily amount, take it with other drugs containing acetaminophen, or have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using the product. That warning appears on acetaminophen-based Midol too.

### The doubling-up trap is the real danger

Most accidental acetaminophen overdoses aren't one big mistake. They're several small ones that add up. Period pain often lasts two or three days, and people take a dose, then another, then reach for a different product without checking what's in it. Common examples:

- Taking Midol Complete for cramps and **Tylenol** for a headache on the same day.
- Taking Midol during the day and **Midol PM, Tylenol PM, or NyQuil** at night.
- Adding a cold and flu product, which very often contains acetaminophen too.
- Taking a prescription painkiller that contains acetaminophen, such as hydrocodone or oxycodone combinations.

The daily limit covers acetaminophen from **every** source combined. If you've had a few drinks on top of that, the margin for error shrinks. Follow the per-dose and per-day limits printed on your specific box, keep a simple running tally, and don't treat Midol as "just a period pill" that doesn't count toward your acetaminophen total.

## Ibuprofen or Naproxen Midol and Alcohol: The Stomach and Kidney Risk

Some Midol products use ibuprofen (the drug in Advil and Motrin) or naproxen sodium (the drug in Aleve) instead of acetaminophen. These belong to a family called NSAIDs, short for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. They're often genuinely good at period cramps, because they reduce prostaglandins, the chemical messengers that make the uterus contract and cause pain.

They're easier on the liver than acetaminophen, but they bring a different set of problems when alcohol is involved:

- **Stomach irritation and bleeding.** NSAIDs reduce the protective layer that lines your stomach. Alcohol irritates that same lining. Together they raise the risk of indigestion, gastritis, ulcers, and bleeding. That's why NSAID labels carry a stomach-bleeding warning that specifically mentions people who have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day**.
- **Kidney strain.** NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys a little. That usually doesn't matter in a healthy, well-hydrated person. After a night of drinking you're often dehydrated, and that's when the effect matters more.
- **Naproxen lasts longer.** A naproxen dose stays active for up to about 12 hours, so it overlaps with more of your drinking or recovery window than a short-acting painkiller would.

If you do take an ibuprofen or naproxen Midol after drinking, take it **with food and a full glass of water**, stick to the label dose, and stop if you get stomach pain. Skip it entirely and ask a pharmacist if you have a history of ulcers, kidney disease, heart disease, or you take blood thinners or steroid medicines. For more detail, see our guides to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol).

## The Add-Ons: Caffeine, Antihistamines, and Water Pills

The extra ingredients in Midol are where it differs most from a plain bottle of Tylenol or Advil, and they're easy to overlook.

### Caffeine

Many Midol formulas include caffeine, roughly comparable to a small cup of coffee per dose. Caffeine helps some pain relievers work a bit better, and it fights the tiredness that often comes with a period. With alcohol, it causes three problems:

1. **It can mask how drunk you are.** Caffeine makes you feel more alert, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol level or improve your reaction time. Feeling "fine" can lead you to drink more or to drive when you shouldn't.
2. **It disrupts sleep.** Alcohol already makes sleep lighter and more broken in the second half of the night. Adding caffeine late in the evening makes that worse, and poor sleep makes the next day feel much rougher.
3. **It adds to dehydration a little.** The effect is modest, but it stacks on top of alcohol.

We go deeper on this combination in our [caffeine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol).

### Sedating antihistamines (pyrilamine and diphenhydramine)

Pyrilamine maleate shows up in some Midol formulas for bloating, and diphenhydramine (the drug in Benadryl) shows up in "PM" or nighttime versions. Both are older antihistamines that cause drowsiness. Alcohol is a sedative too. The labels on these products tell you to avoid alcoholic drinks because alcohol can increase the drowsiness.

In practice, combining them can leave you far more sleepy, clumsy, and foggy than you'd expect from either alone. That raises the risk of falls and accidents and makes driving dangerous. It's also a bad combination for anyone who has been drinking heavily, because sedatives on top of a lot of alcohol can slow breathing. Our [antihistamines and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) covers this in more depth.

**Midol PM is the version to be most careful with.** It typically pairs acetaminophen with diphenhydramine. That means a liver interaction and a sedation interaction in the same pill, taken at bedtime, which is exactly when people are most likely to have just been drinking. Don't take a PM product on a night you drink.

### Pamabrom (water pill)

Pamabrom is a mild diuretic used in some menstrual products to relieve bloating by helping you pass water. Alcohol is also a diuretic. Together they can leave you more dehydrated, which can worsen headache, dizziness, and the general hangover feeling. If your product contains pamabrom, drink extra water and don't count on it to help with the puffy, bloated feeling that alcohol itself can cause.

## Midol for a Hangover: Does It Help?

Some people reach for Midol the morning after because it's what's in the cabinet, or because they figure "complete" relief must cover a hangover too. It's not designed for hangovers, and it's not a great choice for one.

- **The pain reliever only helps the headache and body aches.** There's no good evidence that acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or naproxen improves the other parts of a hangover, such as nausea, fatigue, or that general sick feeling.
- **The acetaminophen versions carry extra liver load** at a time when, for people who drink heavily, the liver may be least able to handle it.
- **The NSAID versions can make an already-irritated stomach worse,** and hangover nausea and heartburn are common enough without help.
- **The caffeine may help a little with grogginess,** but it won't fix the underlying causes, which include dehydration, poor sleep, and the by-products of alcohol breakdown.
- **The antihistamine versions can leave you groggier,** which is the opposite of what you want.

If you have a headache the morning after and you want a pain reliever, a plain single-ingredient product lets you take only what you need. Our comparison of [Advil vs Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) walks through the trade-offs. And if your hangover shows up with a lot of nausea, pick something gentle and eat first.

## Drinking During Your Period: Why the Timing Is Tricky

Searches for "Midol and alcohol" spike for an obvious reason: periods don't schedule themselves around weekends, birthdays, or holidays. It's worth knowing that the period itself can change how alcohol affects you.

- **Cramps can get worse.** Alcohol can contribute to dehydration and may make cramps and headaches feel worse for some people.
- **Bloating can get worse.** Many people already retain water before and during their period, and alcohol can add to puffiness.
- **Mood and sleep take a hit.** Alcohol disrupts sleep, and poor sleep makes mood swings and fatigue more noticeable.
- **Heavy bleeding and NSAIDs.** NSAIDs are often recommended for heavy periods because they can reduce flow, but heavy drinking can affect blood clotting. If you have very heavy periods, that's a reason to talk with your doctor about the best plan.

For more on this, see our guide to [how alcohol affects your period](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-affect-your-period).

None of this means you can't have a drink during your period. It means the same night out may hit harder, and it's a reason to plan your pain relief rather than reaching for whatever's nearby at midnight.

## How to Use Midol More Safely Around Drinking

These are general, practical steps for healthy adults. They aren't personal medical advice.

1. **Read the Drug Facts box first.** Identify the pain reliever (acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or naproxen) and any add-ons (caffeine, antihistamine, pamabrom).
2. **Don't take it while you're drinking.** Take your period pain relief earlier in the day, before you start, and then don't re-dose until the alcohol has cleared.
3. **Wait until the alcohol is out of your system before the next dose.** There's no universal official waiting time. As a rough guide, the body clears about one standard drink per hour, but this varies a lot. After a heavy night, that can mean well into the next day.
4. **Eat something first.** Food protects your stomach from NSAIDs and helps your liver with acetaminophen.
5. **Take one standard dose, not a stack.** More pills won't make cramps or a headache go away faster. They only add risk.
6. **Count every product.** Keep track of acetaminophen from Midol, Tylenol, cold medicines, and sleep aids combined.
7. **Skip the PM versions on drinking nights.** The sedation stacks.
8. **Drink water.** Alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and have a full glass with any dose.
9. **Use non-drug help too.** A heating pad or hot water bottle on the lower belly is a well-established way to ease cramps, and it doesn't interact with anything.

## Safer Alternatives for Cramps When You've Been Drinking

If you know you'll be drinking and you're worried about cramps, a few options can reduce how much medicine you need:

- **Heat.** Heat patches and heating pads are a simple, drug-free option with decent evidence behind them for period cramps.
- **Timing your NSAID earlier.** NSAIDs tend to work best for cramps when started early, before the pain gets bad. Taking a dose with a meal earlier in the day, well before you drink, may mean you don't need one later.
- **Light movement and stretching.** Gentle exercise helps some people with cramps.
- **Talk to your doctor about recurring severe cramps.** If cramps are severe enough that you need painkillers every month, it's worth a conversation. Hormonal birth control and other treatments can help, and severe pain can sometimes point to conditions such as endometriosis that deserve proper care.

## When to See a Doctor or Get Help Right Away

Most people who take a normal dose of Midol after a few drinks will be fine. But some signs need attention.

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or go to the emergency room if:**

- You may have taken more acetaminophen than the label allows, from Midol alone or combined with other products, even if you feel fine. Early acetaminophen poisoning can feel like nothing much, or like a hangover, and the damage shows up later. The hospital antidote works best when it's started early.
- Someone who has been drinking heavily took a sedating (PM) product and is very hard to wake, confused, or breathing slowly. Call 911.

**See a doctor promptly if you notice:**

- Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
- Black, tarry, or bloody stools
- Severe or persistent stomach pain
- Yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs
- Much less urine than usual, or swelling in your legs
- Period pain that is severe, getting worse month to month, or unlike your usual cramps

**Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using Midol at all if you:**

- Drink 3 or more drinks most days
- Have liver disease, kidney disease, stomach ulcers, or a history of stomach bleeding
- Take blood thinners, steroids, certain blood pressure medicines, antidepressants, or sedatives
- Are pregnant or breastfeeding

For a broader look at how common medicines and supplements interact with alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Where DHM Fits, Honestly

Midol treats period symptoms. It does nothing for the effects of alcohol, and depending on the formula it can add to your liver's or stomach's workload after drinking. If you're looking this up because you often wake up after a night out needing a painkiller, the most effective steps are the unglamorous ones: drink less, drink slower, eat beforehand, and alternate with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also try **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers reliably in people, and it does **not** change how you should use Midol or any other painkiller. It doesn't make acetaminophen safer with alcohol, and it doesn't protect your stomach from ibuprofen or naproxen. If you want to try it, take it separately from your period medicine and follow the same label rules regardless. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when.

## The Bottom Line

- "Midol" covers several different formulas. Check the Drug Facts box to see whether yours contains **acetaminophen**, **ibuprofen**, or **naproxen**, plus any **caffeine**, **antihistamine**, or **pamabrom**.
- **Acetaminophen Midol** carries a liver risk with alcohol, especially with high doses, doubling up with other acetaminophen products, fasting, or regular heavy drinking.
- **Ibuprofen or naproxen Midol** carries a stomach-bleeding and kidney risk with alcohol, especially on an empty stomach or when dehydrated.
- **Caffeine** can mask how drunk you feel and hurt your sleep. **Antihistamines** stack drowsiness. **PM versions** combine a liver risk and a sedation risk, so skip them on drinking nights.
- Don't take Midol while drinking or "pre-emptively" at bedtime. Wait until the alcohol has cleared, eat, take one standard dose, and count every product.
- If there's any chance of an acetaminophen overdose, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take Midol after drinking alcohol?**

For most healthy adults who don't drink heavily day to day, one standard dose the morning after a few drinks is unlikely to cause harm. First check which Midol you have: acetaminophen versions carry a liver risk with alcohol, while ibuprofen or naproxen versions carry a stomach and kidney risk. Wait until the alcohol has cleared, eat something, and follow the label. If you have 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

**Does Midol have acetaminophen in it?**

Some Midol products do and some don't. Midol Complete has long combined acetaminophen with caffeine and an antihistamine, and PM versions typically pair acetaminophen with a sleep aid. Other Midol products use ibuprofen or naproxen sodium instead. The only reliable way to know is to read the active ingredients in the Drug Facts box on your box.

**How long after drinking can I take Midol?**

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. A sensible approach is to wait until the alcohol is out of your system (the body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot), eat first, and then take a single standard dose. Don't take Midol while you're actively drinking or at bedtime to get ahead of cramps or a hangover.

**Can I drink alcohol on my period if I took Midol earlier?**

If you took a normal dose earlier in the day, an occasional drink later is unlikely to cause problems for most healthy adults, but the safest plan is not to re-dose until the alcohol has cleared. Avoid PM versions on drinking nights, because the sleep aid adds to alcohol's drowsiness. If your Midol contains acetaminophen, count it toward your daily total and don't add Tylenol or cold medicines on top.

**Is Midol PM safe with alcohol?**

It's the version to be most careful with. Midol PM typically combines acetaminophen with diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine. That means a liver interaction and a drowsiness interaction at the same time, usually taken at bedtime right after drinking. The label tells you to avoid alcohol while using it. Skip it on any night you drink.

**Does the caffeine in Midol cancel out alcohol?**

No. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol level or improve your judgment or reaction time. Feeling more awake can lead people to drink more or drive when they shouldn't. Caffeine late at night also makes alcohol's sleep disruption worse.

**Is Midol good for a hangover?**

It's not designed for hangovers. The pain reliever in it may ease a headache, but there is no good evidence that it helps nausea, fatigue, or the other parts of a hangover. Acetaminophen versions add liver load and ibuprofen or naproxen versions can irritate an already upset stomach. If you only need headache relief, a plain single-ingredient product lets you take just what you need.

**What are the warning signs after taking Midol and alcohol?**

Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) right away if you may have taken too much acetaminophen, even if you feel fine. See a doctor promptly for vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, severe stomach pain, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or much less urine than usual. Call 911 if someone who has been drinking heavily is very hard to wake or breathing slowly after taking a sedating product.
